results.title: Not Merely Averages: Using Machine Learning to Estimate Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (CATE, BLP, GATES, CLAN) | by Lucas Kitzmüller | TDS Archive | Medium
results.content: *This blog post provides a practical introduction on how to use generic machine learning inference on heterogeneous treatment effects in experiments as proposed by* *Chernozhukov, Demirer, Duflo and Fernández-Val (2020).* *I wrote this blog post for the statistically minded practitioner who is interested in applying the method in their work. A traditional approach to estimating treatment effect heterogeneity is splitting the sample (e.g., male vs. **(2)** **Complex treatment effect heterogeneity.** Even if you pre-register your analysis, traditional sample splits have another disadvantage: they don’t capture complex, higher-order interactions between treatment and baseline characteristics. **Over the past years, researchers have developed new tools that rely on machine learning methods to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects in a disciplined fashion.** An early and still popular approach is Honest Causal Forest by Wager & Athey (2017). Taking the difference gives us the estimated individual treatment effects.** (The general intuition here is that with ML methods we can model the ‘true’ underlying relationship between baseline characteristics and treatment status on one hand and the outcome on the other hand and therefore can predict what an individual’s outcome would have been if it were in the other group.). Using these predicted individual treatment effects, we then analyze the following three properties to learn about treatment effect heterogeneity. Therefore, testing if β₂ is statistically significantly different from zero is our first test of treatment effect heterogeneity (and our ML methods detecting it).**. We can compare how different ML methods perform in predicting treatment effects over 100 runs, and focus on the best-performing ones. We also see there is no difference in the variables which we did not use when we created the treatment effect heterogeneity in our data (plotting variable z10 as an example). So should I just always using generic machine learning to estimate treatment effect heterogeneity?**. Therefore, if you have a clear sense from the beginning of what characteristics are most relevant for treatment effect heterogeneity (e.g., based on theory or existing studies), pre-specifying these groups and using traditional methods is still your best bet.

results.title: User Guide — DoubleML documentation
results.content: # User Guide#. The basics of double/debiased machine learning. Regularization bias in simple ML-approaches. Overcoming regularization bias by orthogonalization. Sample splitting to remove bias induced by overfitting. Difference-in-Differences Models (DID). Group average treatment effects (GATEs). Conditional average treatment effects (CATEs). Conditional value at risk (CVaR). Implementation of the score function and the estimate of the causal parameter. Implemented Neyman orthogonal score functions. Specifying alternative score functions via callables. Implementation of the double machine learning algorithms. Learners, hyperparameters and hyperparameter tuning. Variance estimation and confidence intervals. Confidence bands and multiplier bootstrap for valid simultaneous inference. Simultaneous inference over different DoubleML models (advanced). Sample-splitting, cross-fitting and repeated cross-fitting. Cross-fitting with *K* folds. Repeated cross-fitting with *K* folds and *M* repetitions. Externally provide a sample splitting / partition. Sample-splitting without cross-fitting. Estimate DML models without sample-splitting.

results.title: A Tutorial Introduction to Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Estimation with Meta-learners | Administration and Policy in Mental Health and Mental Health Services Research
results.content: We focus on meta-learners because they are straightforward to implement in standard statistical software and also very flexible by allowing to incorporate standard statistical models (e.g., the generalized linear model) and/or popular machine learning algorithms (e.g., random forests, gradient boosted trees, neural networks) to estimate heterogeneous treatment effects.Footnote 1 Psychotherapy research has increasingly focused on treatment effect heterogeneity and individual treatment recommendations in the past decade (see e.g., Barber & Muenz 1996. Meta-learners are algorithms that decompose CATE estimation into multiple prediction problems, each of which can be solved by any machine learning model, and then combine the results of these models to obtain \({\hat{\tau }}({\varvec{x}})\) (Künzel et al., 2019. The weighting serves to pull the final estimate closer to the estimated effect that relies on the conditional mean function estimated in the larger group (i.e., that is expected to be more accurate).Footnote 11 Similar to the X-learner, the DR-learner and the R-learner estimate the CATE by modelling a pseudo-outcome as a function of the covariates, which can remove some of the bias induced by regularization and overfitting compared to the S-learner and the T-learner (Curth & van der Schaar, 2021.

results.title: [PDF] Meta-Learners for Estimation of Causal Effects: Finite Sample Cross ...
results.content: In this paper, we study the ﬁnite sample performance of meta-learners for estimation of heterogeneous treatment eﬀects under the usage of sample-splitting and cross-ﬁtting to reduce the overﬁtting bias. Keywords: Meta-learners, causal machine learning, heterogeneous treatment eﬀects, Monte Carlo simulation, sample-splitting, cross-ﬁtting. In this paper, we address both of the above issues and study the ﬁnite sample properties of the machine learning based meta-learners for the estimation of causal eﬀects based on the speciﬁc implemen-tations using the full-sample, sample-splitting and cross-ﬁtting procedures for varying sample sizes. However, the most prominent and widely used meta-learners in the literature consist of the more complex X-learner (K¨ unzel et al., 2019), the DR-learner (Kennedy, 2020), and the R-learner (Nie & Wager, 2021), which all require prior estimation and combi-nation of several nuisance functions, such as the conditional means of the outcome and the treatment, 1In the marketing literature the so-called uplift modelling is concerned with the same target of estimating causal eﬀects and developed in parallel to the classical econometric and causal machine learning literature. Figure 1 illustrates this theoretical argument by contrasting the distributions of the CATE parameter under full-sample estimation, double sample-splitting and double cross-ﬁtting, resulting from a Monte Carlo simulation based on a large training sample of 32′000 observations (further details on the meta-learner and the simulation design are provided in Sections 3.2 and 4, respectively). 15 In order to objectively evaluate the performance and the robustness of diﬀerent meta-learners in estimating heterogeneous treatment eﬀects with regard to the double sample-splitting and double cross-ﬁtting, we design several simulation scenarios. 5 Discussion Given the results of our synthetic and semi-synthetic simulations there are several important ﬁndings for the estimation of heterogeneous causal eﬀects by the meta-learners and the associated usage of sample-splitting and cross-ﬁtting which are relevant for applied empirical work. Among the meta-learners based on the estimation of nuisance functions, the X-learner performs very well not only in settings with highly unbalanced but also in less unbalanced treatment shares with simple CATEs and demonstrates the theoretically argued capability to learn such CATE structures (K¨ unzel et al., 2019).
